content.rendered:
THE National Assembly’s decision to extend, for a third time, the implementation of the capital component of the 2025 Appropriation Act, from June 30 to September 30, 2026, is yet another symptom of the chaos that has come to define Nigeria’s budget cycles under the Bola Tinubu administration.

Nigeria’s public finance management system has long been plagued by weak planning, poor execution capacity, unrealistic projections, and a persistent inability to align budget promises with implementation realities.

However, since 2023, these failures appear to be amplifying rather than being contained.

The House of Representatives justified the latest extension as necessary to prevent the abandonment of ongoing projects.

House Leader Julius Ihonvbere argued that failure to extend the budget would have “a very grave impact on the growth and development of the national economy.”

Speaker Tajudeen Abbas similarly noted that available records showed that implementation of the capital budget remained incomplete and required additional time.

 The Senate, on its part, agrees.

While there is logic in ensuring that ongoing infrastructure projects are not abandoned midway, the recurring resort to budget extensions raises troubling questions about governance and fiscal discipline.

This is the third extension granted to the 2025 capital budget after previous rollovers approved in December 2025 and March 2026. What was initially presented as an exceptional measure has now become standard operating procedure.

Indeed, Nigeria is effectively running overlapping budgets simultaneously. Portions of the 2023, 2024, 2025 and now 2026 fiscal frameworks are being implemented concurrently.

 This, to say the least, is absurd.

Such a situation complicates oversight, distorts accountability, and weakens transparency. It means that legislators, auditors, civil society organisations and citizens continue to struggle to determine which projects belong to which budget cycle, how much has actually been spent, and what value has been delivered.

The situation should not be surprising, however. According to budget documents, only about 20 per cent of the 2025 capital allocation, roughly N4.99 trillion out of N24.9 trillion, had been released by mid-year.

Yet capital expenditure remains the engine of infrastructure development, job creation and productivity growth. Roads, hospitals, schools, power projects and other facilities cannot be delivered through recurrent spending.

While funding shortages have been adduced, the deeper issue lies in persistent systemic weaknesses.

In its April 2026 Nigeria Development Update, the World Bank noted that “only 24 per cent of the prorated 2025 capital budget of MDAs was implemented, leaving a significant portion of approved investment unspent and limiting the growth impact of public spending.”

It observed that overall capital spending declined from 1.3 per cent of GDP (N5.5 trillion) in 2024 to 1.0 per cent of GDP (N4.5 trillion) in 2025, despite overall government spending rising to 6.7 per cent of GDP (N29.7 trillion).

This was driven largely by higher personnel costs, rising debt service obligations, and increased intervention spending.

This recurring failure stems from revenue projections often proving overly optimistic; procurement processes remain cumbersome and slow, and capital fund releases are frequently delayed.

MDAs routinely submit ambitious project lists far beyond available resources, apart from lawmakers’ often frivolous insertions. Weak monitoring mechanisms and bureaucratic bottlenecks further undermine implementation.

The consequences for productivity and economic growth are severe. Infrastructure projects are delayed, contractors remain unpaid, and economic benefits that should accrue from completed projects are postponed indefinitely.

Businesses depend on predictable fiscal signals and functioning infrastructure. When budget implementation becomes erratic, investment decisions are disrupted, logistics costs rise, and productivity suffers.

The fiscal implications are just as worrisome. Nigeria’s public debt has climbed to approximately N153 trillion, while debt servicing consumes an increasingly large share of government revenue.

The 2026 fiscal framework projects debt service costs of N15.52 trillion and a deficit exceeding N20 trillion.

Extending budgets without addressing underlying implementation failures merely prolongs expenditure commitments while increasing pressure on public finances.

Still, the extension is not without benefits. It provides contractors awaiting payments and project approvals with an opportunity to complete ongoing work and prevents waste from abandoning partially completed projects.

It also offers government agencies a final window to utilise already appropriated funds for projects that may yet yield economic and social benefits.

However, these short-term advantages cannot obscure the larger governance failure. Budget extensions should be rare exceptions, not recurring features of fiscal management. Every rollover weakens the integrity of the January-to-December budget cycle painstakingly restored in recent years under the Buhari administration.

Nigeria’s budgeting challenge is obviously institutional. The solution lies in realistic revenue projections, stricter adherence to statutory timelines, faster procurement processes, improved project monitoring, and transparent publication of implementation reports.

The NASS must strengthen oversight rather than just approve extensions. Questions need to be asked about why this has become a recurring decimal, and if the 2026 budget implementation is not already imperilled, as well.

Equally important, the executive must ensure that appropriated funds translate into measurable outcomes.

A budget is not judged by the size of its appropriations but by the quality of its execution.

Therefore, Nigeria must confront the structural deficiencies that necessitate repeated extensions. Otherwise, budget rollovers will remain a costly hallmark of governance failure rather than a tool for development.
